newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco talks focus on liability issues.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco talks focus on liability issues.

text.p: State attorneys general and cigarette makers were to resume talks on Tuesday to consider several proposals, including one that would limit how much the tobacco industry would pay annually for smokers' injuries.

The attorneys general said they were optimistic about meeting with industry representatives, saying that a jury verdict in favour of R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. in a trial in Jacksonville, Fla., on Monday would not affect their negotiations.

After meeting late into Monday evening in small groups, the state legal officers resumed their discussions at about 9 a.m. EDT, two hours before they were scheduled to meet tobacco company representatives.
One of the negotiators told Reuters that the attorneys general had suggested several proposals over the past few days on how to deal with the difficult issue of liability.
The states want to give the industry an incentive to settle, but refuse to agree to total immunity.

The attorneys general have sued the industry to recoup Medicaid costs of smokers. But the negotiations also include plaintiffs lawyers representing individual smokers and representatives of the health community.
The negotiator said that one of the proposals would set up a fund with an annual limit, which would allow the industry to know how much to set aside each year.

If a smoker is successful in a lawsuit against the industry and the fund for that year is low or already has been exhausted, the plaintiff would still get paid, but the full amount might not be received until the following year, the source said.
"This is just one of the proposals. There are other things on the table," the source said.

Following the session with tobacco representatives Monday, Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore, a key player in the talks, said that the industry had made new concessions but emphasised that there would be no blanket immunity.
He said the state lawyers were organised into five working groups to consider separate issues, including whether there is insurance to cover claims against the industry.
In Jacksonville, Fla., a jury Monday cleared R.J. Reynolds of responsibility for the death of a smoker who died of lung cancer.

The jury deliberated for eight hours over two days before deciding Reynolds had neither acted negligently nor made a dangerous, defective product that caused the death of Jean Connor, who smoked heavily from the time she was a teenager and died of lung cancer in October 1995 at age 49.

Despite the verdict, tobacco company stocks were lower Tuesday after gaining sharply on Monday. RJR lost $1.125 to $31.50 and Philip Morris was off $1.125 at $42.875, both in heavy trading on the New York Stock Exchange. In contrast, Loews Corp. gained $1.625 to $97.25, also on the NYSE.
